direct_answer: Older and frail people are more at risk in hot weather. Keeping cool, drinking regularly, planning activity for cooler times and checking on others help. Some medicines affect how the body handles heat. Heat exhaustion needs prompt cooling, and heatstroke is an emergency.
author: Louis Maxwell

content:
Hot weather can be risky for older and frail people, particularly those living alone or with several health conditions.

This guide covers staying safe in a heatwave. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Staying cool

  • Keep curtains closed on sunny windows.
  • Stay out of the sun between 11am and 3pm.
  • Use a fan, cool showers or damp cloths.
  • Wear loose, light clothing.

Drinking enough

  • Drink regularly, even if not thirsty.
  • Keep drinks within easy reach, in a cup that is easy to hold.
  • If you have been told to limit fluids, ask your GP for advice.

Medicines and heat

Some medicines, such as diuretics or some blood pressure medicines, can affect how you cope with heat. Do not stop medicines, but ask your pharmacist for advice. Store medicines as directed.

Signs of heat exhaustion

Headache, dizziness, nausea, cramps, heavy sweating, and feeling very thirsty. Move somewhere cool, drink and cool down. Call 999 if still unwell after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, being cooled and drinking fluids.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for heatstroke signs such as confusion, fits, loss of consciousness, very high temperature, fast breathing or shortness of breath, a fast heartbeat, or hot skin that is not sweating. Do not wait for every sign. Keep cooling the person while waiting for help.
  • Call 999 if still unwell after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, being cooled and drinking fluids. Do not wait longer or use NHS 111 instead at this point.
  • Contact NHS 111 if you are struggling to treat heat exhaustion or need advice before that emergency threshold. In Northern Ireland, contact your GP or GP out-of-hours service for urgent advice.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Does heat affect arthritis?

Some people notice changes. Heat-related illness is the main concern in frailty.

Who should I check on?

Older neighbours, especially those living alone.
